metin: This one'll be quicker.
In first grade, the teacher held up three pencils and said, "Count them." But I'd already seen it without counting.
That day I kept wondering: if my eyes can see it, why do we count? Who came up with numbers, and what for?
Then my notebook filled up with digits, but nobody ever answered that question.
That was the question left unanswered that day: why do we count? Today I won't give you the answer. You'll find it yourself.
Where do we start? There aren't even any numbers here yet.
We start with your eyes, because numbers begin exactly where your eyes stop being enough.
Don't count. Just look. Which one had more?
The right one. I didn't even think.
This time… I don't know. They seemed the same.
The left one had 100, the right one 110. The first time the difference was 10. This time it's 10 too.
The difference is the same. But the first time it was half the pile; this time it got lost in the crowd.
Three pencils, or the baskets at the store, there was no crowd to get lost in. That's why my eyes knew without counting.
But now my question is even bigger: if the eye is that good, why did we ever need counting?
Because of a job the eye can't do. Come on, you do that job.
Imagine this: numbers don't exist yet, and you're a shepherd.
In the morning your sheep leave the pen one by one and spread out over the pasture.
Easy. They graze until evening, then they come back.
Evening's here, the sheep are back. Did all of them come home?
It looks about the same… but I couldn't even tell 100 from 110. If one were missing, would I notice?
And this time that one sheep matters: a missing sheep spends the night outside, all alone.
Then "about the same" isn't good enough. I need to know exactly.
Wait, I've got an idea. I'll give every sheep a name and call the names one by one in the evening.
Nice. But in the evening, will you remember all twenty names?
…I'd mix them up by the third one. Then I'll line the evening flock up next to the morning flock, find a partner for every sheep, and the one without a partner shows what's missing.
Good idea. So where's the morning flock now?
The morning flock… is this flock. The ones who left this morning are the very same ones coming back. There's no second flock to line them up with.
So I have to keep this morning's amount somewhere until evening.
Where would you keep it? No paper, no pen, no number words. All you have is what's lying around you.
A stone! Every morning, for each sheep that goes out, I drop a stone in the pouch.
In the evening, for each sheep that comes back, I take one out. If a stone is left in the pouch, a sheep is still out there.
One stone left. I've left one outside!
You found it without knowing a single number.
I just made that up. Did people really do this?
In Iraq, near Kirkuk, in the ancient city of Nuzi, archaeologists found a hollow clay container about 3,500 years old.
The writing on it lists 48 sheep and goats handed over to a shepherd. And inside, there were 48 small stones.
That's exactly my pouch, just made of clay!
This pot isn't the first stone; people may have counted with stones much earlier. But it shows your idea was really used.
Counting with stones became so common that the stone's name became the word for counting: the Romans called a small stone "calculus", and that's where the word "calculate" comes from.
Calculator… my calculator is named after a pebble?
Yes. The calculator on your phone is a great-grandchild of that shepherd's pouch.
But I can't carry a bag of stones everywhere.
You can't. That's why people found other tools that do the stone's job. You use one every day: number words.
When you say "twenty", you're carrying twenty stones, not in your pocket, but on your tongue.
So the digits they gave us at school were a tool like that too. But I always struggled with that tool. I was always slow at math. Am I stupid?
No.
You were handed the tool itself, but nobody ever showed you what problem it solves. A tool you've never seen at work feels strange in anyone's hands.
It might be hard, but it's not meaningless. Today we saw the problem numbers solve, together. We'll look at the next tools the same way.
I saw the three pencils without counting, because three is small and my eyes were enough.
Numbers are for where my eyes aren't enough: for what isn't in front of me, for what I have to carry exactly from morning to evening.
If I'd had sheep, I'd have found a way too. In fact, I just did: the stone. The digits in my notebook are that stone, carried forward.
You won't always have a bag of stones with you. But there are ten things you carry everywhere.
My fingers… I've always counted with these. I never thought of them as stones.
Next stop: Fingers and Body.
What was the question you could never ask at school? Write it in the comments. We read every one when planning the next stops.
